hints: Focus on what structure an alcohol needs to give a positive iodoform test with alkaline iodine.
Check which alcohol contains the $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)}-$ group, which is first oxidised to a methyl carbonyl $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}-$.
Remember the cleavage always gives yellow $\text{CHI}_3$ plus a carboxylate ion from the rest of the molecule, so count the carbons left behind.
walkthrough:
**Recall the iodoform condition**

Great start, let us remember the rule together. Alkaline $\text{I}_2$ gives a yellow precipitate of $\text{CHI}_3$ only with a methyl carbonyl $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}-$ group or an alcohol that can be oxidised to one.

For alcohols, that means: $$\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)}- \text{ group must be present}$$

**Test each alcohol**

Now let us look at the structures. Propan-2-ol is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)CH}_3$, so it has the $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)}-$ unit and will react.

Propan-1-ol is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$, so it lacks that unit and gives no reaction. Butan-2-ol is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)CH}_2\text{CH}_3$, so it also has the unit and will react.

**Predict the correct products**

Here is the clever part. The $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}-$ part becomes iodoform, $\text{CHI}_3$, and the rest of the molecule, R, becomes $\text{RCOO}^-$.

For propan-2-ol via propanone $\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_3$: $$\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_3 + 3\text{I}_2 + 4\text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{COO}^- + \text{CHI}_3 + 3\text{I}^- + 3\text{H}_2\text{O}$$ So the pair $\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-$ and $\text{CHI}_3$ is exactly correct.

options.A: Butan-2-ol does give a positive test, but the products are wrong. The formula $\text{CH}_3\text{CI}_3$ is a trap, it mixes up chlorine with iodine and adds an extra carbon, the iodoform is $\text{CHI}_3$. Also cleavage of butan-2-one gives propanoate, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COO}^-$, not ethanoate.
options.B: Propan-1-ol, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$, does not contain the $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)}-$ group and cannot be oxidised to a methyl ketone. It gives a negative iodoform test, so it cannot form $\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-$ and $\text{CHI}_3$.
options.C: Propan-2-ol, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)CH}_3$, contains the key $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)}-$ group. It is oxidised to propanone then cleaved by alkaline iodine to give ethanoate, $\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-$, and yellow iodoform, $\text{CHI}_3$. This matches perfectly.
options.D: Butan-2-ol does form $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COO}^-$, because the R group left after cleavage is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2-$. However the second product must be iodoform, $\text{CHI}_3$, not iodomethane, $\text{CH}_3\text{I}$. This confuses substitution with the haloform cleavage.
